brave-llmcontext.snippet:
#### § 1104.7 Computation and extension of time.
(a) *Computation.* In computing any period of time, the day of the act, event, or default upon which the designated period of time begins to run is not included. The last day of the period is included unless it is Saturday, Sunday, or a legal holiday in the District of Columbia, in which event the period runs until the end of the next day which is not a Saturday, Sunday or holiday. This rule applies to forward and backward measurement of time.
(b) *Extensions.* Any time period, except those provided by law or specified in these rules respecting informal complaints seeking damage, may be extended by the Board in its discretion, upon request and for good cause. Requests for extensions must be served on all parties of record at the same time and by the same means as service is made on the Board. However, if service is made on the Board in person and personal service on other parties is not feasible, service on other parties should be made by first class or express mail.
A request for an extension must be filed not less than 10 days before the due date, except that in cases seeking expedited relief for service emergencies under part 1146 of this chapter, a request for an extension must be made within 24 hours of service of the petition, reply, or other filing or procedural order of the Board as applicable. Only the original of the request and certificate of service need be filed with the Board.
If granted, the party making the request should promptly notify all parties to the proceeding of the extension and so certify to the Board, except that this notification is not required in rulemaking proceedings.

exa.snippet:
# Title 49 

#### § 1104.7 Computation and extension of time.

(a) Computation. In computing any period of time, the day of the act, event, or default upon which the designated period of time begins to run is not included. The last day of the period is included unless it is Saturday, Sunday, or a legal holiday in the District of Columbia, in which event the period runs until the end of the next day which is not a Saturday, Sunday or holiday. This rule applies to forward and backward measurement of time.

(b) Extensions. Any time period, except those provided by law or specified in these rules respecting informal complaints seeking damage, may be extended by the Board in its discretion, upon request and for good cause. Requests for extensions must be served on all parties of record at the same time and by the same means as service is made on the Board. However, if service is made on the Board in person and personal service on other parties is not feasible, service on other parties should be made by first class or express mail. A request for an extension must be filed not less than 10 days before the due date, except that in cases seeking expedited relief for service emergencies under part 1146 of this chapter, a request for an extension must be made within 24 hours of service of the petition, reply, or other filing or procedural order of the Board as applicable. Only the original of the request and certificate of service need be filed with the Board. If granted, the party making the request should promptly notify all parties to the proceeding of the extension and so certify to the Board, except that this notification is not required in rulemaking proceedings.

(c) Exception to time computation rules. See 49 CFR part 1152 for special abandonment rules.

# 29 CFR § 2700.9 - Extensions of time. 

§ 2700.9 Extensions of time.

(a) The time for filing or serving any document may be extended for good cause shown. Filing of a motion requesting an extension of time is effective upon receipt. A motion requesting an extension of time shall be received no later than 3 days prior to the expiration of the time allowed for the filing or serving of the document, and shall comply with § 2700.10. The motion and any statement in opposition shall include proof of service on all parties by a means of delivery no less expeditious than that used for filing the motion, except that if service by email or other electronic transmission is impossible, the filing party must serve in person, or by third-party commercial carrier, resulting in same-day delivery.

jina.title: FMCSA wants to lengthen time limit for emergency-related HOS exemptions
jina.snippet:
Washington — The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration is asking for feedback as it considers extending hours-of-service exemption periods for truckers during regional emergency declarations.

Under a proposal [published](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/01/09/2026-00268/clarification-to-the-applicability-of-emergency-exemptions-response-to-petitions-for-reconsideration) Jan. 9, FMCSA would exempt drivers and motor carriers from HOS regulations for 30 days. That’s up from the 14 days allotted in a [final rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/10/13/2023-22538/clarification-to-the-applicability-of-emergency-exemptions) that went into effect in December 2023. The proposal was issued in response to petitions for reconsideration of the rule.

The exemption was good for 30 days before the [2023 rule](https://www.safetyandhealthmagazine.com/articles/24724-fmcsa-final-rule-scales-back-scope-of-regulatory-relief-during-emergencies) was effective and covered all regulations in 49 CFR Parts 390-399.

In the proposal, FMCSA cites “uncertainty” related to the length of emergency exemptions and points to multiple recent events in which relief extended beyond 14 days, including wildfires in the western United States and successive hurricanes in North Carolina in fall 2024.

jina.snippet:
Date: January 09, 2026 | Author: [Land Line Media](https://landline.media/author/land_line_media/) | Category: [Federal](https://landline.media/category/federal/), [News](https://landline.media/category/news/)

Emergency declarations and the regulatory relief that comes with these orders could soon see a change.

In a [notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/01/09/2026-00268/clarification-to-the-applicability-of-emergency-exemptions-response-to-petitions-for-reconsideration) of proposed rulemaking published on Friday, Jan. 9, the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration proposed revising the length of emergency relief automatically triggered by a declaration of emergency from 14 days to 30 days.

FMCSA said the proposal is in response to [petitions](https://landline.media/ooida-national-propane-gas-association-ask-fmcsa-to-adopt-emergency-rule-petition/) for reconsideration of a final rule published in October 2023.

Those revisions narrowed the scope of the safety regulations from which relief is automatically provided when an emergency is declared. It limited the automatic exemption to 14 days of hours-of-service relief for eligible motor carriers and drivers.

The previous regulation provided a 30-day automatic exemption from all regulations in 49 CFR Parts 390-399. For local emergencies, limited to five days, this exemption covered only hours of service in sections 395.3 and 395.5.

OOIDA, the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance, the Montana Department of Transportation and the National Propane Gas Association were among the petitioners.

### **FMCSA said the majority of the petitions requested the agency reconsider the 14-day time limit, noting that it was too short.**

“In our experience, the current 30-day period provides sufficient time to deliver emergency assistance without negatively impacting safety,” OOIDA wrote in 2023. “We are unclear on exactly why FMCSA is proposing these regulatory changes at this time.”

## **What Is an Emergency Motion for Extension of Time?**  
An emergency motion for extension of time is a formal legal document filed in a court of law before an existing procedural deadline expires, requesting that the court grant additional time to comply with that deadline based on exigent, unforeseeable, or extraordinary circumstances that make compliance within the original timeframe impossible or unjust.
## **Why Do Courts Deny Emergency Motions for Extension of Time?**  
Courts deny emergency motions for extension of time most frequently on four grounds: the movant fails to demonstrate a genuine emergency distinct from ordinary scheduling difficulty, the movant did not contact opposing counsel before filing, the motion lacks a supporting declaration, or the court has already granted one or more prior extensions and finds that further extensions serve no legitimate purpose.
The Ninth Circuit diverges from most other federal circuits in three specific ways. First, it requires the telephonic clerk notification within 24 hours of filing, a requirement absent from the Fifth and Eleventh Circuits' emergency procedures. Second, the Ninth Circuit caps emergency briefing schedule extensions at 35 days beyond the original deadline, whereas other circuits apply a reasonableness standard without a hard cap. seltz.snippet:
Guardianship · Sub-Topic

Fla. Stat. § 744.3031 · Fla. Prob. R. 5.648

Emergency temporary guardianship is the one guardianship proceeding that moves in days rather than months. It is also the one most often misunderstood from both sides: petitioners file it expecting a standalone remedy, and families on the receiving end learn of it only after letters have issued and the accounts are frozen. It requires a pending incapacity petition, a finding of imminent danger, and it expires — 90 days, with one extension.

## What it is

Under Fla. Stat. § 744.3031(1), a circuit court may appoint an emergency temporary guardian of the person, the property, or both, of an alleged incapacitated person. The court must find imminent danger that the physical or mental health or safety of the person will be seriously impaired, or that the person's property is in danger of being wasted, misappropriated, or lost. The powers granted must be specifically listed in the order, and an emergency temporary guardian may not be given more authority than the emergency actually requires.

The gating fact most petitioners miss is that an ETG is not a freestanding proceeding. It may be filed only after a petition to determine incapacity has been filed, and only before a guardian has been appointed (§ 744.3031(1); Fla. Prob. R. 5.648(a)). There is no way to obtain emergency relief over an adult's person or money without also putting their capacity at issue — which is a serious step, and the right first conversation to have. The narrow exception runs the other direction: under § 744.3031(3), where no guardianship petition has been filed by the time an order determining incapacity is entered, the court may appoint an emergency temporary guardian on its own motion.

seltz.snippet:
**The Pennsylvania Mental Health Procedures Act (MHPA) is the 1976 state law, codified at 50 P.S. § 7101 et seq., that governs how Pennsylvania handles psychiatric emergencies, from voluntary treatment to involuntary commitment. It sets strict legal standards for when someone can be detained against their will, spelling out who can file a petition, how long detention can last, and what rights patients keep throughout the process.** Nearly fifty years later, it still shapes what happens the moment a mental health crisis becomes a legal one.

The Pennsylvania Mental Health Procedures Act is the state’s foundational mental health law, passed in 1976 to replace a patchwork of inconsistent, often arbitrary commitment practices with a structured legal process. Before the Act, there was no reliable statewide standard for deciding when someone could be hospitalized against their will, or what rights they kept once they were.

The law does two things at once. It creates pathways for people to get psychiatric treatment, both voluntarily and involuntarily, and it builds in safeguards so that involuntary treatment doesn’t become a rubber stamp for locking people away. Every provision in the Act, from emergency evaluation to extended commitment, exists inside that tension: how do you protect public safety without steamrolling individual liberty?

That tension isn’t unique to Pennsylvania.
